rv.q: The result is a performance marked by a delicate interplay of charm, emotional nakedness, and raw theatrical intensity.

It’s a lot to weave into a single act, and Stachel, along with Taccone and dramaturg Madeleine Oldham, have landed on a lean script performed with charm, vulnerability, and moments that push catharsis to the brink of exorcism.
I’m glad he gets a stage on which to say it.
Ari’el Stachel’s one-man show is a deeply personal and brutally honest portrayal of anxiety, set against the backdrop of his troubled relationship with identity.
He never asks for pity, places blame, or makes excuses, but bravely and honestly reveals his scars, shows us his wounds, and involves us in his process of healing.
Good on him, but that’s not compelling enough to sustain a 90-minute solo routine.

cn.t: Tony winner Stachel delivers a brave, intensely honest solo show about anxiety and identity that critics find gripping and unsettling. His charisma shines through despite—or because of—the raw vulnerability on display.
